chunks: IMU definition and tradeoffs. The question: What is an inertial measurement unit (IMU)? What are its tradeoffs?
An IMU, or inertial measurement unit, is one small package that holds motion sensors so a device can tell how it is moving and which way it is pointing.
The usual minimum is an accelerometer and a gyroscope, each measuring along three directions. Choosing one is a trade-off between noise, drift, range, speed, power and cost.
Think of a bathroom scale and a laboratory balance. Both measure weight, but the lab balance is far more precise and far more expensive.
To check a suitcase, the bathroom scale is fine. IMUs span a similar ladder, from phone chips costing a few dollars to aircraft units costing tens of thousands.
The scale picture leaves out that an IMU must also fit the data link to the processor, the power budget and the mounting.
A modern IMU is a small system: two MEMS sensors, ADCs, digital filtering, calibration constants, buffering and sometimes a processor, all behind a serial bus and interrupt lines.
Features like free-fall detection run on-chip so the host can sleep.
Axis: one direction of measurement. A 6-axis IMU has three accelerometer axes and three gyroscope axes.
A 9-axis one adds a magnetometer, which senses the Earth's magnetic field to find heading. Drift: a small error that grows as you add up readings over time.
Range: the largest input the sensor can read before clipping. Output data rate: how many readings per second the IMU produces.
Free-run: relying on the IMU alone, with no outside correction such as GPS.
Say a device must free-run for 10 minutes and keep its heading within 1 degree. Ten minutes is one sixth of an hour.
So the gyroscope's drift must stay under 1 degree divided by one sixth of an hour, which is 6 degrees per hour.
A phone-grade part, with tens to hundreds of degrees per hour, cannot do that on its own. An industrial part, at roughly 1 to 10 degrees per hour, can. That is the whole idea.
"An IMU packages a three-axis accelerometer and gyroscope, often plus a magnetometer and barometer, to measure motion and orientation.

The trade-offs: noise versus bandwidth versus power, bias stability which sets how long you can free-run, range versus resolution, bus bandwidth for the output rate, and the vibration, temperature and magnetic environment.
Consumer MEMS gyros drift tens of degrees per hour or more, navigation-grade ones thousands of times less, at orders of magnitude more cost."
